decks.title: Diseases and their Transmission — Part 1: Kinds of disease, spread, and bacterial diseases
goals: Classify diseases as communicable or non-communicable, and use the terms endemic, epidemic, pandemic and sporadic
Explain how diseases spread through air, water and insect vectors
State the symptoms and control of cholera, typhoid and tuberculosis

slides.heading: Diseases and their Transmission
slides.body_md: Part 1 — what a disease is, how it spreads, and three bacterial diseases.

visual.alt: Flow from a pathogen through a route of spread to a new host who falls ill

slides.narration: A disease is a condition that stops the body from working properly. Many diseases are caused by tiny living things called pathogens. In this part we see how pathogens travel from one person to another, and we study three diseases caused by bacteria.

slides.heading: Communicable and non-communicable diseases

rows: A pathogen such as a bacterium, virus, protozoan or worm
Not a pathogen: lifestyle, deficiency, heredity or ageing
Passes from a sick person or animal to a healthy person
Does not pass from person to person

visual.alt: Table comparing communicable and non-communicable diseases by cause, spread and examples

slides.narration: Communicable diseases are caused by pathogens and can pass from one living thing to another. Non-communicable diseases cannot be caught. They arise from causes such as poor diet, heredity or a body part wearing out. Cholera is communicable, while diabetes is not.

slides.heading: Endemic, epidemic, pandemic and sporadic

rows: Always present in a particular area or population
A disease found in every year in one district
Suddenly affects many people in an area at the same time
A sharp rise in cholera in a town
Epidemic that spreads over many countries or continents
A flu that spreads across the world
A few scattered cases at irregular times, no common source
A few typhoid cases in different towns

visual.alt: Table of the four patterns of occurrence of a disease with meaning and example

slides.narration: These four words describe how a disease occurs. Endemic means always present in one area. Epidemic means a sudden rise in cases in an area. Pandemic means an epidemic spread across many countries. Sporadic means a few scattered cases with no common source.

slides.heading: Quick check: a sudden rise
slides.body_md: A disease that suddenly affects a large number of people in one area at the same time is
slides.narration: Think about the word that means a sudden rise in one area.

slides.heading: Worked example 1: is it an epidemic?
slides.body_md: A town normally records 4 cases of a disease in a month. In one month it records 92 cases. How many times the usual number is this, and what is the pattern?
bullets: Step 1: times the usual = 92 ÷ 4 = **23**.
Step 2: extra cases = 92 − 4 = **88**.
Step 3: a sudden rise in one area far above the usual is an **epidemic**.

visual.alt: Worked table: ninety-two cases is twenty-three times the usual four, an epidemic

slides.narration: Divide this month by the usual number. Ninety-two divided by four gives twenty-three, so there are twenty-three times as many cases as usual. That is eighty-eight extra cases. A sudden jump in one town is an epidemic.

slides.heading: How pathogens travel

rows: Droplets from a cough or sneeze are breathed in
Pathogens in drinking water or uncovered food are swallowed
An animal, usually an insect, carries the pathogen
Touch, blood, needles or sexual contact
AIDS, hepatitis B, chicken pox blisters

visual.alt: Table of four routes by which pathogens travel with diseases for each

slides.narration: Pathogens travel in several ways. Through the air in droplets from a cough. Through water and food that has been contaminated. Through vectors, which are animals that carry them. And through contact, blood or body fluids.

slides.narration: A housefly feeds on waste and dirt. Germs stick to its legs and body. When the fly lands on uncovered food, the germs are left behind, and the person who eats the food may fall ill.

slides.heading: Vectors: housefly, mosquito and cockroach

rows: Carries germs on legs and body from waste to food
Cover food, dispose of waste safely, keep drains closed
Bites a sick person, then a healthy one; breeds in stagnant water
Drain stagnant water, use nets and repellents
Walks over waste, then over food and utensils
Keep kitchens clean and food covered

visual.alt: Table of the vectors housefly, mosquito and cockroach with how they spread disease and the control

slides.narration: The housefly and the cockroach carry germs on their bodies from waste to food. The mosquito bites a sick person and then a healthy one, and it breeds in stagnant water. Control means clean surroundings, covered food and no standing water.

slides.heading: Quick check: a vector
slides.body_md: An animal that carries a pathogen from one host to another, without itself being the cause of the disease, is a
slides.narration: The mosquito and the housefly are examples.

slides.heading: Worked example 2: tracing the source
slides.body_md: Ward P (2000 people) drinks from a broken pipe and has 48 cases of typhoid. Ward Q (2500 people) uses a covered well and has 5 cases. Which ward points to a contaminated water source?
bullets: Step 3: P has **12 times** the rate of Q, so the **broken pipe** is the likely source.

visual.alt: Worked table comparing cases per thousand people in ward P and ward Q

slides.narration: Compare the wards by cases in every thousand people, not by raw numbers, because the wards differ in size. Ward P has twenty-four in every thousand. Ward Q has two. The rate in P is twelve times higher, which points to the broken pipe.

slides.heading: Cholera and typhoid

rows: Sudden, severe watery diarrhoea, vomiting, cramps, loss of water from the body
Long-lasting fever that rises step by step, headache, weakness, stomach pain
Boiled or chlorinated water, oral rehydration, clean food, safe disposal of waste, vaccine
Boiled water, hygiene, clean food, fly control, vaccine, antibiotics on a doctor's advice

visual.alt: Table comparing cholera and typhoid by pathogen, spread, symptoms and control

slides.narration: Cholera and typhoid are both caused by bacteria and spread through contaminated water and food. Cholera causes sudden severe watery diarrhoea and loss of body water. Typhoid causes a long fever, headache and weakness. Boiled water and clean food help control both.

slides.heading: Tuberculosis

rows: Bacterium that mainly infects the lungs
Through the air, in droplets from the cough of a patient
Cough lasting weeks, sometimes with blood, chest pain, tiredness, weight loss, evening fever
Cover the mouth when coughing, good ventilation, vaccine in childhood, full course of the prescribed antibiotics

visual.alt: Table of the pathogen, spread, symptoms and control of tuberculosis

slides.narration: Tuberculosis is caused by a bacterium that mainly infects the lungs. It spreads through the air in droplets from the cough of a patient. A cough lasting weeks, weight loss and tiredness are signs. A full course of medicine is essential.

slides.heading: Quick check: an airborne disease
slides.body_md: Which of these diseases spreads mainly through droplets in the air?
slides.narration: Think about the lungs.

slides.heading: Summary
bullets: Communicable diseases are caused by pathogens and can spread; non-communicable diseases cannot.
Endemic, epidemic, pandemic and sporadic describe how a disease occurs.
Routes: air, water and food, vectors, contact.
Cholera and typhoid: water and food. Tuberculosis: air.

visual.alt: Summary table of cholera, typhoid and tuberculosis with route and key control

slides.narration: To recap. Communicable diseases are caused by pathogens and can spread. Endemic, epidemic, pandemic and sporadic describe how a disease occurs. Pathogens travel by air, water and food, vectors and contact. Cholera and typhoid spread in water and food, and tuberculosis spreads in the air.

slides.heading: Exam tips
bullets: Give an **example** with every term: **endemic, epidemic, pandemic, sporadic**.
Name the **route of spread** for each disease and the **vector** where there is one.
Write **symptoms** and **control measures** as separate short points.
Do not write scientific names of the pathogens; the syllabus does not ask for them.
slides.narration: Exam tips. Give an example with each term. Name the route of spread for each disease, and the vector where there is one. Write symptoms and control as separate short points. Scientific names of pathogens are not needed.

decks.title: Diseases and their Transmission — Part 2: Viral, protozoan and helminthic diseases
goals: State the symptoms, spread and control of AIDS, chicken pox and hepatitis
State the symptoms and control of malaria, amoebic dysentery and sleeping sickness
State the symptoms and control of ascariasis, taeniasis and filariasis

slides.heading: Viruses, Protozoans and Worms
slides.body_md: Part 2 — nine more diseases, grouped by the kind of pathogen.

visual.alt: Flow showing the three groups of pathogens in this part: viruses, protozoans and worms

slides.narration: This part covers nine diseases in three groups. Three are caused by viruses, three by single-celled protozoans, and three by worms. For each one we learn how it spreads, what its signs are and how it is controlled.

slides.heading: AIDS

rows: A virus that attacks the white blood cells of the immune system
The body can no longer fight many germs, so common infections become serious
Long fever, weight loss, swollen glands, long diarrhoea, repeated infections
Safe blood, new or sterilised needles, safe sexual practices, medical care in pregnancy, awareness

visual.alt: Table of the pathogen, effect, symptoms and control of AIDS

slides.narration: AIDS is caused by a virus that attacks the white blood cells of the immune system. The body then cannot fight even common germs. Signs include long fever, weight loss and swollen glands. It is controlled by safe blood, clean needles and awareness.

slides.heading: How AIDS spreads and how it does not

rows: Unprotected sexual contact with an infected person
Hugging, shaking hands or sitting together
Sharing food, utensils or a toilet
From an infected mother to her baby

visual.alt: Table contrasting the ways AIDS spreads with ways it does not spread

slides.narration: The virus passes through certain body fluids, mainly in blood and in sexual contact, and from a mother to her baby. It does not spread through hugging, shared food, toilets, coughs or mosquitoes. Knowing this helps us support patients without fear.

slides.heading: Quick check: the target of the virus
slides.body_md: The virus that causes AIDS mainly damages the body's
slides.narration: The virus attacks the defence system.

slides.heading: Chicken pox and hepatitis

rows: Air droplets; touching the fluid of blisters
Type A: food and water; type B: blood, needles, body fluids
Mild fever, then itchy red spots that become fluid-filled blisters and scab
Tiredness, loss of appetite, yellow skin and eyes (jaundice), dark urine
Isolate the patient, rest, hygiene, vaccine
Boiled water and clean food, vaccine, safe blood, sterile needles

visual.alt: Table comparing chicken pox and hepatitis by pathogen, organ, spread, symptoms and control

slides.narration: Chicken pox and hepatitis are viral. Chicken pox affects the skin and gives itchy blisters, and it spreads through the air and by touch. Hepatitis affects the liver and causes yellow skin and eyes. Type A spreads through food and water, and type B through blood.

slides.heading: Quick check: yellow skin

slides.narration: This sign is called jaundice.

slides.narration: A female Anopheles mosquito bites a person with malaria and sucks blood with the parasites. When it bites a healthy person it passes the parasites on. The mosquito lays its eggs in stagnant water, where the young develop.

slides.heading: Malaria: symptoms and control

rows: A protozoan that lives in red blood cells and the liver
Chills, then high fever and sweating, repeating at regular intervals; headache; weakness; anaemia
Drain stagnant water, spray oil or insecticide, keep fish that eat larvae, use nets and screens
Medicines for malaria, on a doctor's advice

visual.alt: Table of the pathogen, symptoms, vector control and treatment of malaria

slides.narration: Malaria is caused by a protozoan that lives in the liver and red blood cells. The patient has chills, then high fever and sweating, repeating at regular intervals. We control it by removing stagnant water, using nets and treating patients early.

slides.heading: Worked example 1: the rhythm of the fever
slides.body_md: A malaria patient has fever peaks on days 3, 6 and 9. How many days apart are the peaks and on which day is the next expected?
bullets: Step 1: gap = 6 − 3 = **3** days; 9 − 6 = **3** days as well.
Step 2: next peak = 9 + 3 = **day 12**.
Step 3: fever returning at regular intervals is a feature of **malaria**.

visual.alt: Worked table of fever peaks on days three, six and nine with the next expected on day twelve

slides.narration: Find the gap between peaks. Six minus three is three, and nine minus six is three. The peaks are three days apart. Add three to nine, and the next peak is expected on day twelve. Regular fever is typical of malaria.

slides.heading: Worked example 2: draining the breeding places
slides.body_md: A colony has 12 water containers with 50 mosquito larvae in each. Residents empty 9 of them. By what percentage do the larvae fall?
bullets: Step 2: containers left = 12 − 9 = 3; larvae after = 3 × 50 = **150**.
Step 3: fall = 450 ÷ 600 × 100 = **75 per cent**.

visual.alt: Worked table: six hundred larvae fall to one hundred fifty, a fall of seventy-five per cent

slides.narration: Before, twelve containers with fifty larvae each hold six hundred larvae. After emptying nine, three containers remain, so one hundred fifty larvae are left. The fall is four hundred fifty out of six hundred, which is seventy-five per cent.

slides.heading: Amoebic dysentery and sleeping sickness

rows: Protozoan living in the large intestine
Protozoan living in the blood and later the brain
Food and water with the resting stage; flies
Bite of the tsetse fly, found in parts of Africa
Diarrhoea with blood and mucus, stomach cramps
Fever, headache, swollen glands, then constant sleepiness
Boiled water, washed hands, covered food, safe disposal of faeces, fly control, medicines
Control of tsetse flies, early treatment

visual.alt: Table comparing amoebic dysentery and sleeping sickness by pathogen, spread, symptoms and control

slides.narration: Amoebic dysentery is caused by a protozoan in the large intestine. It spreads through food and water and gives diarrhoea with blood and mucus. Sleeping sickness is caused by a protozoan carried by the tsetse fly. It brings fever and then constant sleepiness.

slides.narration: This fly is found in parts of Africa.

slides.heading: Helminthic diseases: worms

rows: Eggs in soil, water and unwashed vegetables
Stomach pain, poor growth, anaemia, worms in stool
Wash hands and vegetables, safe latrines, medicine
Stomach discomfort, weight loss, pieces of worm in stool
Cook meat well, meat inspection, medicine
Thread-like worms in the lymph vessels
Fever, swelling of legs and other parts (elephantiasis)

visual.alt: Table of ascariasis, taeniasis and filariasis with the worm, spread, symptoms and control

slides.narration: Three diseases are caused by worms. Ascariasis is caused by a roundworm whose eggs reach us in soil, water and unwashed vegetables. Taeniasis comes from a tapeworm in undercooked meat. Filariasis is caused by thread-like worms, spread by mosquitoes, and causes swollen legs.

slides.narration: The mosquito is the vector.

slides.heading: Summary
bullets: Viral: AIDS (white blood cells), chicken pox (skin), hepatitis (liver).
Protozoan: malaria (mosquito), amoebic dysentery (food and water), sleeping sickness (tsetse fly).
Helminthic: ascariasis (roundworm), taeniasis (tapeworm), filariasis (mosquito).

rows: Safe blood and needles, vaccine, hygiene
Clean food, cooked meat, mosquito control

visual.alt: Summary table of the three groups with their diseases and main control

slides.narration: To recap. AIDS, chicken pox and hepatitis are viral. Malaria, amoebic dysentery and sleeping sickness are protozoan. Ascariasis, taeniasis and filariasis are caused by worms. For each, link the pathogen, the way it spreads and the control.

slides.heading: Exam tips
bullets: Write **female Anopheles** for malaria and **Culex** for filariasis when the vector is asked.
For AIDS, say what it **does** (attacks white blood cells) and how it **spreads and does not spread**.
Give **two control measures** for each disease, and match them to the route.
Do not say that antibiotics cure viral diseases.

sections.heading: 1. Communicable and non-communicable diseases; how diseases occur
sections.body_md:
A **disease** is a condition in which the body or a part of it does not work properly. Diseases are of two broad kinds.

| | **Communicable** | **Non-communicable** |
|---|---|---|
| Cause | A **pathogen** (bacterium, virus, protozoan, worm) | Not a pathogen: poor diet or lifestyle, deficiency, heredity, ageing |
| Spread | Passes from a sick person or animal to a healthy one | **Cannot** be caught from another person |
| Examples | Cholera, typhoid, tuberculosis, AIDS, malaria | Diabetes, scurvy, cancer, heart disease |

**How a disease occurs in a population**
- **Endemic**: always present in a particular area or population.
- **Epidemic**: a sudden rise in the number of cases in an area, in a short time.
- **Pandemic**: an epidemic that spreads over many countries or across the world.
- **Sporadic**: a few scattered cases at irregular times, with no common source.

Textbooks give different examples for these terms (for instance, which disease is called endemic in which place); what matters is the pattern, and an example should always agree with the meaning.

key_terms.definition_md: A disease that can spread from one living thing to another.
A sudden rise in the number of cases of a disease in an area.
An epidemic spread over many countries.

sections.heading: 2. Modes of transmission: air, water and vectors
sections.body_md:
Pathogens spread by four main routes.

| Route | How | Diseases in this chapter |
|---|---|---|
| **Air** | Tiny droplets from a cough or sneeze are breathed in | Tuberculosis, chicken pox |
| **Water and food** | Pathogens in unsafe water or uncovered food are swallowed | Cholera, typhoid, amoebic dysentery, hepatitis A, ascariasis |
| **Vectors** | An animal, usually an insect, carries the pathogen | Malaria, filariasis, sleeping sickness; flies and cockroaches for gut diseases |
| **Contact and body fluids** | Touch, blood, shared needles, sexual contact, mother to child | AIDS, hepatitis B, chicken pox (blisters) |

**Vectors**
- **Housefly:** feeds on waste; germs stick to its legs and body and are left on food.
- **Mosquito:** female **Anopheles** carries malaria; **Culex** carries filariasis. Mosquitoes breed in stagnant water.
- **Cockroach:** walks over waste, then over food and utensils.
- **Tsetse fly** carries sleeping sickness (parts of Africa).

**General control:** safe drinking water, covered food, hygienic disposal of waste, no standing water, cough hygiene and good ventilation.

key_terms.definition_md: An animal that carries a pathogen from one host to another.
Spread of a pathogen in tiny drops from a cough or sneeze.

sections.heading: 3. Bacterial diseases: cholera, typhoid and tuberculosis
sections.body_md:
Scientific names of the pathogens are not required in this syllabus.

| | **Cholera** | **Typhoid** | **Tuberculosis** |
|---|---|---|---|
| Spread | Contaminated water and food; flies | Contaminated water and food; flies | Air, by droplets from a patient's cough |
| Symptoms | Sudden severe **watery diarrhoea**, vomiting, cramps, loss of body water (dehydration) | **Long-lasting fever** rising step by step, headache, weakness, stomach pain | **Cough lasting weeks**, sometimes with blood, chest pain, weight loss, evening fever, tiredness |
| Control | Boiled or chlorinated water, **oral rehydration**, clean food, safe disposal of waste, vaccine | Boiled water, hygiene, clean food, fly control, vaccine, antibiotics on a doctor's advice | Cover the mouth when coughing, ventilation, **vaccine** in childhood, a **full course** of the prescribed antibiotics |

In cholera the greatest danger is the loss of water and salts, so the patient is given a solution of salts and sugar in water (oral rehydration) while the doctor treats the infection. A tuberculosis patient must finish the whole course of medicine even after feeling better.

Vaccines against cholera and typhoid are used in some situations and their use is decided by health authorities (as of 2026); the safest general protection is safe water and clean food.

key_terms.definition_md: Loss of too much water and salts from the body.
Giving water with salts and sugar by mouth to replace what is lost.

sections.heading: 4. Viral diseases: AIDS, chicken pox and hepatitis
sections.body_md:
| | **AIDS** | **Chicken pox** | **Hepatitis** |
|---|---|---|---|
| Pathogen | A virus that attacks the **white blood cells** of the immune system | A virus | Viruses of several types (A, B and others) |
| Organ affected | The immune system | The skin | The **liver** |
| Spread | Unprotected sexual contact, infected blood, shared needles, mother to baby | Air droplets; touching the fluid in the blisters | Type A: contaminated food and water; type B: blood, needles, body fluids |
| Symptoms | Long fever, weight loss, swollen glands, long diarrhoea, repeated infections | Mild fever, then itchy red spots that become fluid-filled **blisters** and form scabs | Tiredness, loss of appetite, **jaundice** (yellow skin and eyes), dark urine |
| Control | Screened blood, new or sterilised needles, safe sexual practices, awareness | Isolate the patient, rest, hygiene, vaccine | Boiled water, clean food, vaccine, screened blood, sterile needles |

**AIDS does not spread** by hugging, handshakes, sharing food or utensils, toilets, coughs, sneezes or mosquito bites. The virus makes the body unable to fight other infections, and it is these infections that make the patient seriously ill. Medicines can keep the virus under control but there is no cure (as of 2026). **Antibiotics do not act on viruses.**

key_terms.definition_md: A disease in which a virus damages the immune system so that the body cannot fight infections.
Yellowing of the skin and eyes, a sign of liver disease.

sections.heading: 5. Protozoan diseases: malaria, amoebic dysentery and sleeping sickness
sections.body_md:
| | **Malaria** | **Amoebic dysentery** | **Sleeping sickness** |
|---|---|---|---|
| Pathogen | A protozoan that lives in the liver and red blood cells | A protozoan that lives in the large intestine | A protozoan that lives in the blood and later the brain |
| Spread | Bite of the **female Anopheles** mosquito | Food and water contaminated with the resting stage; flies | Bite of the **tsetse fly** (parts of Africa) |
| Symptoms | **Chills, then high fever and sweating** at regular intervals; headache; weakness; anaemia | **Diarrhoea with blood and mucus**, stomach cramps | Fever, headache, swollen glands, then constant sleepiness and confusion |
| Control | Drain stagnant water, oil or insecticide on breeding places, fish that eat larvae, nets, screens, repellents, early treatment | Boiled water, washed hands and vegetables, covered food, safe disposal of faeces, fly control, medicines | Control of tsetse flies, early treatment |

Malaria is not caught by touching a patient; the mosquito must first bite a patient and then a healthy person. The regular rise of fever is a clue that points to malaria.

key_terms.definition_md: A single-celled organism, some of which cause disease.

sections.heading: 6. Helminthic diseases: ascariasis, taeniasis and filariasis
sections.body_md:
Helminths are parasitic worms.

| | **Ascariasis** | **Taeniasis** | **Filariasis** |
|---|---|---|---|
| Worm | **Roundworm**, in the small intestine | **Tapeworm**, in the intestine | **Thread-like** filarial worms in the lymph vessels |
| Spread | Eggs in soil, water and unwashed vegetables; dirty hands | Eating **undercooked** meat that holds the larval stage | Bite of the **Culex** mosquito |
| Symptoms | Stomach pain, vomiting, poor growth, anaemia, worms in the stool | Stomach discomfort, weight loss, pieces of worm in the stool | Fever, swelling of the legs and other parts (**elephantiasis**) |
| Control | Wash hands and vegetables, safe latrines, boiled water, medicine | Cook meat well, meat inspection, medicine | Remove stagnant water, nets, repellents, medicine |

Books differ on the finer points of symptoms; the pattern to remember is the route (mouth for the first two, mosquito for the last), the organ affected and a control that blocks the route.

key_terms.definition_md: Great swelling of a limb caused by blocked lymph vessels in filariasis.

notes.exam_tips_md:
**Common mistakes**
- Mixing up **epidemic** (sudden, one area) and **pandemic** (many countries).
- Saying a **vector causes** the disease; it only **carries** the pathogen.
- Writing that **AIDS spreads by touch**, hugging, food or mosquitoes.
- Saying that **antibiotics** cure viral diseases such as chicken pox or hepatitis.
- Giving **scientific names** of pathogens (not required); naming the **vector** (female Anopheles, Culex, tsetse fly) is required.

**How marks are usually awarded**
- 1 mark: a term, an odd one out **with its category**, a give-reason item.
- 2 marks: two symptoms, or two control measures, or a vector and the disease.
- 3 marks: a three-row comparison, or symptoms, spread and control.
- 10-mark structured question: a short situation or diagram with parts of 2 to 4 marks; one part is a labelled diagram.

questions.stem_md: Village M has 3000 people and 60 cases of a disease. Village N has 5000 people and 70 cases. By how many cases in every 1000 people is the rate in M higher than the rate in N?
questions.solution_md: M: 60 ÷ 3000 × 1000 = 20. N: 70 ÷ 5000 × 1000 = 14. Difference = 6. (N has more cases, but M has the higher rate.)

questions.stem_md: State one difference between a communicable and a non-communicable disease and give one example of each.

answer.model_answer_md: A **communicable** disease is caused by a **pathogen** and **can spread** from one person to another (for example, cholera). A **non-communicable** disease is **not caused by a pathogen** and cannot be caught (for example, diabetes).

questions.solution_md: Pathogen and spread; one example each.

questions.stem_md: Differentiate between an epidemic and a pandemic.

answer.model_answer_md: An **epidemic** is a sudden rise in the number of cases of a disease in **one area**. A **pandemic** is an epidemic that spreads over **many countries** or the whole world.

questions.solution_md: One area versus many countries.

questions.stem_md: Tabulate three differences between an endemic disease and a sporadic disease.

answer.model_answer_md:
| Endemic disease | Sporadic disease |
|---|---|
| **Always present** in an area | Appears **at irregular times** |
| Affects **many people** over time in the same place | Affects **only a few** people |
| Cases often have a **common cause** in the place | Cases are **scattered** with no common source |

questions.solution_md: Presence in time; number affected; source.

questions.stem_md: Name two insect vectors and state one disease spread by each.

answer.model_answer_md: The **housefly** spreads **cholera** (or typhoid or dysentery). The **mosquito** spreads **malaria** (or filariasis). (The cockroach spreads food-borne diseases.)

questions.solution_md: Two vectors with a disease each.

questions.stem_md: Explain how a housefly can spread a disease of the intestine, and state one way of preventing it.

answer.model_answer_md: The fly feeds on **waste** and **germs stick to its legs and body**; it then lands on **uncovered food** and leaves the germs there. It is prevented by **covering food** or by disposing of waste safely.

questions.solution_md: Germs carried from waste to food; cover food.

questions.stem_md: Name three routes by which pathogens spread and give one disease for each.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. Through the **air**, in droplets from a cough or sneeze, as in **tuberculosis**.
2. Through **water and food** contaminated with pathogens, as in **cholera** or typhoid.
3. Through a **vector** such as a mosquito, which carries the parasite from a patient, as in **malaria**. (Also **blood and body fluids**, as in AIDS.)

questions.solution_md: Three routes with a disease each.

questions.stem_md: Tabulate three differences between a housefly and a mosquito as carriers of disease.

answer.model_answer_md:
| Housefly | Mosquito |
|---|---|
| Picks up germs on its **legs and body** from waste | Takes the pathogen in with **blood** from a patient |
| Leaves them on **food** | Passes them by a **bite** |
| Spreads **cholera**, typhoid | Spreads **malaria**, filariasis |

answer.model_answer_md: **Vector.**

questions.solution_md: Vector.

questions.stem_md: True or false? A vector is the organism that causes the disease.
questions.solution_md: False. A vector only carries the pathogen; the pathogen causes the disease.

questions.stem_md: A female mosquito lays 3 batches of 120 eggs on stagnant water. How many eggs does she lay in all?
A boy has passed many watery stools and looks weak, with sunken eyes. The first thing to give him by mouth is

options.text_md: a glass of unboiled pond water
a solution of salts and sugar in clean water

questions.solution_md: Oral rehydration solution replaces the lost water and salts — option (d).

questions.stem_md: A girl has a fever that is a little higher each evening for a week, with headache and weakness, after meals at a roadside stall. The disease is most likely
questions.solution_md: A long fever rising step by step, after unsafe food, suggests typhoid — option (b).

questions.stem_md: A man with tuberculosis feels well after one month of medicine and wants to stop it. The doctor should advise him to

options.text_md: complete the full course of medicine
stop, because the cough is gone
take the medicine only when he coughs
take double doses for a week and then stop

questions.solution_md: Stopping early can leave bacteria alive and the disease may return — option (a).

questions.stem_md: A man has a cough lasting several weeks, with blood in the sputum, and has lost weight. The organ most likely infected is the
questions.solution_md: These are signs of tuberculosis of the lungs — option (b).

questions.stem_md: State two symptoms of cholera and why it is dangerous.

answer.model_answer_md: Cholera causes sudden **watery diarrhoea** and **vomiting** (and cramps). It is dangerous because the body loses a great deal of **water and salts** (dehydration).

questions.solution_md: Diarrhoea and vomiting; dehydration.

questions.stem_md: State how tuberculosis spreads and one measure by which a patient can protect others.

answer.model_answer_md: It spreads through the **air** in **droplets** from the cough of a patient. A patient should **cover the mouth when coughing** (or take the full course of medicine).

questions.solution_md: Droplets; cover the mouth.

questions.stem_md: State how typhoid spreads, two of its symptoms and one measure of control.

answer.model_answer_md: It spreads through **contaminated water and food**, and by **flies**. Its symptoms are a **long-lasting fever** and **headache** (or weakness, stomach pain). It is controlled by **boiled water**, hygiene and clean food (or the vaccine).

questions.solution_md: Contaminated water and food; fever and headache; boiled water.

questions.stem_md: Tabulate three differences between cholera and tuberculosis.

answer.model_answer_md:
| Cholera | Tuberculosis |
|---|---|
| Spreads through **water and food** | Spreads through **droplets in the air** |
| Affects the **intestine**; watery diarrhoea | Affects the **lungs**; long cough |
| **Oral rehydration** and safe water help | A **full course of medicine** and ventilation help |

questions.solution_md: Spread; organ and symptom; control.

questions.stem_md: Give reason: a person with tuberculosis should cover the mouth and nose when coughing.

answer.model_answer_md: The germs leave the body in **droplets** that other people can **breathe in**, so covering the mouth stops them from spreading in the air.

questions.solution_md: Droplets in the air.

questions.stem_md: Give reason: a patient with cholera is given plenty of fluid containing salts.

answer.model_answer_md: The watery diarrhoea makes the body **lose water and salts**, so they must be **replaced** to prevent dehydration.

questions.solution_md: Replaces lost water and salts.

questions.stem_md: A patient with cholera passes 10 watery stools in a day, about 400 mL in each. How many litres of fluid does the body lose?
The evening temperature of a typhoid patient on four days is 38.5, 39.2, 39.8, 40 degrees Celsius. By how many degrees has it risen from the first to the fourth evening?
A tuberculosis patient weighs 54 kg at the start of three months and 48 kg at the end. What is the mean loss of weight each month, in kg?
questions.solution_md: Loss = 54 − 48 = 6 kg; mean = 6 ÷ 3 = 2 kg a month.

questions.stem_md: Which one of these actions carries a risk of passing on the virus that causes AIDS?

options.text_md: Sharing a meal from the same dish
Hugging a friend who is a patient

questions.solution_md: The virus passes in blood, so a shared needle can carry it — option (a).

questions.stem_md: A child has a mild fever, then itchy spots that turn into blisters. To protect the other children at home, the best step is to

options.text_md: give him antibiotics so that he stops being infectious
keep him apart from them until the blisters have dried
let him share a towel with the others
tell him to scratch the blisters

questions.solution_md: Chicken pox spreads by droplets and by touching the blisters, so isolation helps — option (b).

questions.stem_md: A patient has yellow eyes, dark urine and no appetite. The organ affected is the
questions.solution_md: These are signs of hepatitis, an infection of the liver — option (b).

questions.stem_md: A doctor does not prescribe an antibiotic for chicken pox because

options.text_md: chicken pox is caused by a protozoan
chicken pox is caused by a virus, on which antibiotics do not act

questions.solution_md: Antibiotics act on bacteria, not on viruses — option (c).

questions.stem_md: Blood donated in a blood bank is tested for hepatitis B and the virus of AIDS before use, mainly because these infections

options.text_md: are caused by the blood group of the donor
can pass to a patient through transfused blood

questions.solution_md: Screening makes the blood safe — option (d).

questions.stem_md: What does the AIDS virus attack, and why does the patient fall ill so easily?

answer.model_answer_md: It attacks the **white blood cells** of the **immune system**. The body can no longer fight germs, so even **common infections become serious**.

questions.solution_md: White blood cells; cannot fight infections.

marking_scheme.step: White blood cells or immune system

questions.stem_md: State two ways by which AIDS is spread.

answer.model_answer_md: AIDS is spread through **unprotected sexual contact**, **infected blood** in a transfusion, **shared needles**, and from an **infected mother to her baby** (any two).

questions.solution_md: Any two routes.

questions.stem_md: State two symptoms of chicken pox and one way in which it spreads.

answer.model_answer_md: Symptoms: **mild fever** and **itchy red spots** that become **fluid-filled blisters**. It spreads through **droplets in the air** or by touching the fluid of the blisters.

questions.solution_md: Fever, itchy blisters; droplets.

questions.stem_md: Name the organ affected in hepatitis, state two of its symptoms and one way by which hepatitis A spreads.

answer.model_answer_md: Hepatitis is a disease of the **liver**. Its symptoms include **jaundice** (yellow skin and eyes), **dark urine**, tiredness and loss of appetite (any two). Hepatitis A spreads through **contaminated food and water**, for example food handled with unwashed hands.

questions.solution_md: Liver; jaundice and dark urine; food and water.

questions.stem_md: Tabulate three differences between chicken pox and hepatitis.

answer.model_answer_md:
| Chicken pox | Hepatitis |
|---|---|
| Affects the **skin** | Affects the **liver** |
| Itchy **blisters** that form scabs | **Jaundice** and dark urine |
| Spreads by **droplets and blister fluid** | Spreads by **food and water** (type A) or **blood** (type B) |

questions.solution_md: Organ; symptom; spread.

questions.stem_md: Give the biological term: yellowing of the skin and eyes in a patient with liver disease.

answer.model_answer_md: **Jaundice.**

questions.solution_md: Jaundice.

questions.stem_md: Choose the odd one out and name the category to which the other three belong: AIDS, Chicken pox, Hepatitis, Malaria.

answer.model_answer_md: **Malaria**; the others are **viral diseases** (malaria is protozoan).

questions.solution_md: Malaria is protozoan.

questions.stem_md: True or false? A mosquito that bites a patient with AIDS can pass the disease to the next person it bites.
questions.solution_md: False. The virus does not spread by insect bites.

questions.stem_md: A blood bank screens 500 units of donated blood and finds 2 units infected. How many units pass the screening?
A farmer has chills, then a high fever and sweating, and the same cycle returns every third day. The doctor suspects
questions.solution_md: Fever that returns at regular intervals is typical of malaria — option (a).

questions.stem_md: A man passes loose stools with blood and mucus, with stomach cramps, after drinking untreated water. The cause is a protozoan in the
questions.solution_md: This is amoebic dysentery — option (c).

questions.stem_md: A family lives beside a pond. Sleeping under a bed net is useful because it

options.text_md: kills the germs in the pond
keeps mosquitoes from biting at night
kills the flies in the house

questions.solution_md: A net acts as a barrier to the vector — option (b).

questions.stem_md: In the figure, which letter marks the vector that carries the parasites from one person to another?
questions.solution_md: B is the mosquito; A is the infected person, C the stagnant water and D the healthy person — option (a).

questions.stem_md: State two ways of controlling the spread of malaria in a village.

answer.model_answer_md: By **draining or covering stagnant water** (or spraying oil or insecticide) so that mosquitoes cannot breed, and by using **bed nets**, screens or repellents. (Fish that eat larvae may be put in ponds.)

questions.solution_md: Any two measures.

questions.stem_md: State two symptoms of amoebic dysentery and one way of preventing it.

answer.model_answer_md: Symptoms are **diarrhoea with blood and mucus** and **stomach cramps**. It is prevented by drinking **boiled water**, washing hands, covering food and controlling flies.

questions.solution_md: Two symptoms; one preventive measure.

questions.stem_md: Describe the symptoms of malaria and name the vector and the cause of the disease.

answer.model_answer_md: The patient has **chills, then a high fever and sweating**, repeating at regular intervals, with headache and weakness. The vector is the **female Anopheles mosquito**; the disease is caused by a **protozoan** that lives in red blood cells.

questions.solution_md: Symptoms; vector; protozoan.

questions.stem_md: Tabulate three differences between malaria and sleeping sickness.

answer.model_answer_md:
| Malaria | Sleeping sickness |
|---|---|
| Spread by the **female Anopheles** mosquito | Spread by the **tsetse fly** |
| **Regular chills and fever** | Fever, then **constant sleepiness** |
| Found in many warm countries including India | Found in **parts of Africa** |

questions.solution_md: Vector; symptom; place.

questions.stem_md: Give the biological term: a single-celled organism that causes malaria.

answer.model_answer_md: **Protozoan.**

questions.solution_md: Protozoan.

questions.stem_md: Which of these does not belong with the rest: cholera, typhoid, amoebic dysentery, malaria? Give the group to which the others belong.

answer.model_answer_md: **Malaria**; the others spread through **contaminated water and food**.

questions.solution_md: Malaria is spread by a vector.

questions.stem_md: In a village of 150 houses, 105 houses have bed nets. What percentage of the houses has nets?
questions.solution_md: 105 ÷ 150 × 100 = 70 per cent (45 houses have no nets).

questions.stem_md: A meat inspector rejects meat that holds the larvae of a worm, because eating such meat, if undercooked, can cause
questions.solution_md: Tapeworm larvae in undercooked meat cause taeniasis — option (d).

questions.stem_md: Children who play in soil and eat without washing their hands are most at risk of getting
questions.solution_md: Roundworm eggs in the soil reach the mouth on unwashed hands — option (d).

questions.stem_md: A man's leg has become greatly swollen and heavy. The disease is spread by the bite of a
questions.solution_md: Filariasis, which swells the leg, is spread by the Culex mosquito — option (c).

questions.stem_md: Washing raw vegetables well before eating helps to prevent
questions.solution_md: Washing removes the eggs of roundworms — option (b).

questions.stem_md: Name the worm that causes taeniasis and state how a person gets the disease.

answer.model_answer_md: Taeniasis is caused by a **tapeworm** that lives in the intestine. A person gets it by eating **undercooked meat** that holds the larvae of the worm.

questions.solution_md: Tapeworm; undercooked meat.

questions.stem_md: Name the vector of filariasis and the swelling that the disease may cause.

answer.model_answer_md: The vector is the **Culex mosquito**. The disease may cause great swelling of the legs and other parts, called **elephantiasis**.

questions.solution_md: Culex; elephantiasis.

questions.stem_md: State two measures that prevent ascariasis.

answer.model_answer_md: Wash the **hands** before eating and **wash vegetables** well, use **safe latrines** so that faeces do not contaminate soil and water, and drink **boiled water** (any two).

questions.solution_md: Any two measures.

questions.stem_md: Tabulate three differences between ascariasis and taeniasis.

answer.model_answer_md:
| Ascariasis | Taeniasis |
|---|---|
| Caused by a **roundworm** in the small intestine | Caused by a **tapeworm** in the intestine |
| Spread by **eggs** in soil, water and vegetables | Spread by **larvae** in undercooked meat |
| Prevented by **washing hands and vegetables** | Prevented by **cooking meat well** |

questions.solution_md: Worm; source; prevention.

questions.stem_md: A village has several stagnant pools. Name two diseases they may help to spread, and state two measures to deal with the pools.

answer.model_answer_md: Stagnant pools breed mosquitoes that spread **malaria** and **filariasis**. The pools should be **drained or filled**, and **oil or insecticide** sprayed or **larvae-eating fish** introduced where water must stay.

questions.solution_md: Malaria and filariasis; two measures.

questions.stem_md: Choose the odd one out and name the category to which the other three belong: Ascariasis, Taeniasis, Filariasis, Chicken pox.

answer.model_answer_md: **Chicken pox**; the others are **helminthic (worm) diseases**.

questions.solution_md: Chicken pox is viral.

questions.stem_md: Give reason: meat should be cooked thoroughly before it is eaten.

answer.model_answer_md: Thorough cooking **kills the larvae of the tapeworm** that may be present in the meat and so prevents taeniasis.

questions.solution_md: Kills larvae.

questions.stem_md: A sample of vegetables has 80 roundworm eggs on it. After washing, 8 eggs remain. How many times fewer eggs are there after washing?
questions.solution_md: 80 ÷ 8 = 10 times fewer (72 eggs removed).

questions.stem_md:
Select the correct terms to fill in the blanks: [vector, epidemic, jaundice, dehydration, pandemic, endemic, antibiotic, vaccine]

A sudden rise in the number of cases in one town is an (a) ______. An epidemic that spreads over many countries is a (b) ______. An insect that carries a pathogen is a (c) ______. Loss of water and salts from the body in cholera is (d) ______. Yellow skin and eyes in a liver disease is called (e) ______.
questions.solution_md: (a) epidemic; (b) pandemic; (c) vector; (d) dehydration; (e) jaundice.

questions.stem_md: Study the diagram of the spread of malaria and match each lettered part with its description.

match_right.text_md: Route by which the parasites pass to a new person
Person who becomes infected by a bite
Person whose blood holds the parasites
Place where eggs and larvae develop

The bar chart shows the number of new cases in each of six weeks in an outbreak of a disease in a town.

(a) In which week were new cases highest, and how many were there? [2]

(b) Calculate the total number of cases in the six weeks. [2]

(c) Name the pattern of occurrence that this chart shows and give a reason for your answer. [2]

(d) Draw a neat, labelled diagram showing how a housefly can carry germs from waste to food, naming four parts. [4]

**(b)** 2 + 10 + 38 + 66 + 40 + 12 = **168** cases.

**(d)** **Open waste**, a **housefly** with **germs on its legs and body**, **uncovered food**, and an arrow from waste to food; four labels.

Study the diagram, in which a person with a fever, a mosquito and a pool of water are lettered A to E.

(a) Name the parts A, B and C. [3]

(b) Name the disease that spreads in this way and name the cause of the disease. [2]

(c) State two ways in which the spread of this disease can be controlled. [2]

(d) Draw a neat, labelled sketch of a village pond showing three measures that stop mosquitoes from breeding. [3]

answer.model_answer_md:
**(a)** A is the **infected person**, B the **(female Anopheles) mosquito** and C **stagnant water**.

**(b)** **Malaria**; it is caused by a **protozoan** (a parasite that lives in red blood cells).

**(c)** **Drain or cover stagnant water**; use **bed nets** or repellents (or spray oil; introduce larvae-eating fish).

**(d)** A pond with **larvae-eating fish**, a film of **oil** on the water and a **drain** that carries standing water away; three labels.

questions.solution_md: Infected person, mosquito, stagnant water; malaria and a protozoan; two control measures; labelled pond.

questions.stem_md:
In a boarding school of 200 pupils, 18 children get chicken pox in a month. The school sends them to a separate room.

(a) Calculate the percentage of pupils who fell ill. [2]

(b) State two ways in which chicken pox can spread. [2]

(c) Give two reasons for keeping the patients in a separate room. [2]

(d) Draw a neat, labelled diagram of the skin of a patient showing a red spot, a blister and a scab. [4]

answer.model_answer_md:
**(a)** 18 ÷ 200 × 100 = **9 per cent**.

**(b)** Through **droplets in the air** from a cough or sneeze, and by **touching the fluid of the blisters**.

**(c)** To **stop the virus spreading** to the 182 healthy pupils, and so that the patients can **rest** and get care.

**(d)** A patch of skin with a **red spot**, a **fluid-filled blister** and a **scab**; three labels and a title.

After a flood, many people in a village fall ill with sudden watery diarrhoea. One patient passes 10 stools in a day, about 400 mL in each.

(a) Calculate the volume of fluid lost in a day, in litres. [2]

(b) Name the likely disease and state why the patient must be given a solution of salts and sugar in water. [3]

(c) State two measures that the village should take to stop the spread. [2]

(d) Draw a neat, labelled diagram of a protected village well, naming three parts. [3]

answer.model_answer_md:
**(a)** 10 × 400 = 4000 mL = **4 litres**.

**(b)** **Cholera**. The body has lost **water and salts** (dehydration) and these must be **replaced** by **oral rehydration solution**.

**(c)** **Boil or chlorinate drinking water** and **keep food covered**; dispose of waste safely and control flies (any two).

**(d)** A **well with a raised wall and a lid**, a **pump or covered bucket** and a **drain taking spilt water away**; three labels.

questions.solution_md: 4 litres; cholera, replace water and salts; two measures; labelled well.

questions.stem_md:
A health worker tests vegetables from a market. A sample has 80 roundworm eggs before washing and 8 after washing. In the same town, some families have a tapeworm infection and a few have swollen legs.

(a) Calculate how many times fewer eggs there are after washing. [2]

(b) Name the disease caused by the roundworm and state two symptoms. [2]

(c) State how the families got the tapeworm infection and one way of preventing it. [2]

(d) Draw a neat flow diagram showing how undercooked meat can lead to a tapeworm in the intestine, with four labelled steps. [4]

answer.model_answer_md:
**(a)** 80 ÷ 8 = **10 times** fewer.

**(b)** **Ascariasis**; symptoms are **stomach pain** and **poor growth** (or vomiting, anaemia, worms in the stool).

**(c)** By eating **undercooked meat** with larvae; prevented by **cooking meat well** (or meat inspection).

**(d)** **Meat with larvae** → **undercooked meal eaten** → **larva grows in the intestine** → **adult tapeworm**; four labelled steps joined by arrows.

questions.solution_md: 10 times; ascariasis and symptoms; undercooked meat and cooking; flow diagram.
